question: What is the difference between async def and def endpoints in FastAPI?
title: Async vs Sync Endpoints in FastAPI
direct_answer: async def endpoints run in the event loop — use for async I/O (asyncpg, aiohttp, asyncio.sleep). def (sync) endpoints run in a threadpool automatically — FastAPI uses run_in_executor so they don't block the event loop. Never mix: don't call asyncio.run() inside an async endpoint, don't call blocking operations (time.sleep, sync DB) inside async endpoints without asyncio.to_thread(). Use async for async drivers; sync def for blocking operations you can't make async.
interviewer_intent: Tests understanding of when to use async vs sync in FastAPI — a common source of bugs in real projects.

sections.title: async def vs def in FastAPI
sections.content:
FastAPI is an ASGI framework. Its event loop processes all requests. The behavior depends on whether your endpoint is async or sync:

async def endpoint: runs directly in the event loop. Any await suspends and lets other requests proceed. BUT: any blocking call (time.sleep, requests.get, psycopg2 query) blocks the entire event loop and freezes all other requests.

def endpoint (sync): FastAPI automatically runs it in a thread pool (asyncio.run_in_executor with a default thread pool). This means blocking calls in sync endpoints don't block the event loop — the event loop schedules other work while the thread handles the sync call.

So: use async def when you have true async I/O (asyncpg, aiohttp, redis-py async). Use def when you're calling synchronous code that can't be made async (legacy psycopg2, cpu-bound code, some C extensions).

The dangerous anti-pattern: async def with a synchronous database call. Looks like async code, performs like sync, but blocks the event loop for all concurrent requests.

sections.title: Async vs sync patterns
sections.content:
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends
import asyncpg  # async postgres driver
import requests  # sync HTTP — dangerous in async!
import aiohttp   # async HTTP — correct in async

app = FastAPI()

# CORRECT: async endpoint with async I/O
@app.get('/users/{user_id}')
async def get_user_async(user_id: int):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(f'https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}') as resp:
            return await resp.json()   # non-blocking

# WRONG: async endpoint with blocking I/O
@app.get('/users-wrong/{user_id}')
async def get_user_wrong(user_id: int):
    # requests.get is sync — blocks the event loop for ALL requests!
    response = requests.get(f'https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}')
    return response.json()

# OK: sync endpoint — FastAPI runs it in thread pool
@app.get('/users-sync/{user_id}')
def get_user_sync(user_id: int):
    # Blocking call is fine — runs in thread, not event loop
    response = requests.get(f'https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}')
    return response.json()

# If you must use blocking in async: use asyncio.to_thread
import asyncio

@app.get('/users-wrapped/{user_id}')
async def get_user_wrapped(user_id: int):
    # Run blocking call in thread pool without blocking event loop
    response = await asyncio.to_thread(
        requests.get, f'https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}'
    )
    return response.json()

sections.title: async vs sync rules
items: async def: runs in event loop — must use async I/O only
def: FastAPI runs in thread pool — blocking calls are fine
Never: blocking I/O in async def — blocks the entire event loop
asyncio.to_thread(): run blocking code inside async endpoint safely
Async driver stack: asyncpg (postgres), aiohttp (HTTP), redis-py (redis)

seo.metaDescription: Understand FastAPI async vs sync endpoints: async def for async I/O, def for blocking code in thread pool, and asyncio.to_thread for blocking inside async.

speakable_v2.hook: The subtle FastAPI trap: async def with a synchronous requests.get call looks like async code but blocks the entire event loop for all concurrent users.

beats.content: async def runs in the event loop. Every await is a safe suspension point. But any blocking call — time.sleep, a synchronous DB driver, requests.get — freezes the event loop and starves all other requests.
A plain def endpoint runs in a thread pool automatically. FastAPI's run_in_executor means blocking calls are fine — they don't touch the event loop.

Use async def when you have async drivers (asyncpg, aiohttp, async Redis). Use def when you're calling blocking code you can't change. Use asyncio.to_thread() when you need blocking code inside an async function.

speakable_v2.cap: Profiling tip: if your async FastAPI service shows high latency on all endpoints when one is slow, look for a blocking synchronous call inside an async def.
speakable_v2.followup_handoff: Follow up with BackgroundTasks for simple fire-and-forget vs Celery for reliable task queues, or asyncpg setup patterns.
